questions.explanation: #8 separates building and testing, which it says should need no approval, from activation, saying 'We're not looking to push for activation without support'; #1 likewise says activation follows Zcash's existing governance. The tempting wrong reading is that Shielded Labs wants to bypass the community altogether, which #1 and #8 both rule out.
options: Testnets are an ordinary first step of a proposal, so Shielded Labs agreed to hold the first season until coinholders or a community panel had signalled support.
Spinning up a testnet should be permissionless and need no coinholder or panel approval, while mainnet activation would not be pushed without support.
Crosslink's security benefits are important enough that mainnet activation should proceed on technical merit, whatever coinholders or panels say.
Support is a matter for the dev fund process, so the question should wait until the Zcash dev fund extension has been settled.
questions.prompt: dontbeevil suggested that, given the resources going into Crosslink, Shielded Labs should obtain strong signals and support for it (#6). Which of these is the argument made in reply (#8)?

questions.explanation: philthefirst raised the shared-address worry in #54, samhsmith replied in #57 that such nodes mine to their own seed-derived wallet and that tmRB9... is the faucet wallet, and philthefirst accepted this in #60. The snapshot claim stays contested because #55 and #56 found no key material in the archive and #60 does not revisit it. The payout claim is rebutted in #51 and #62, and nobody replied to the mining figures in #87.
options: The public ctaz snapshots ship plaintext secret.seed files that hand their wallet seeds to anyone who downloads them.
alphiz22's 30 Round 1 Orchard staking transactions earned a reward that Shielded Labs failed to pay.
Nodes with no miner_address configured all mine to one shared address, seemingly built into zebrad, that none of them control.
The top ten miners on the feature net hold about 81% of all the cTAZ mined since genesis.
questions.prompt: Which of these claims was conceded by the person who raised it?

questions.explanation: #69 says the servers are up and that what runs on 12301 is UDP, so a TCP check proves nothing; alphiz22 accepts this in #71. #69 does separately suggest the node may be on a side chain or stuck on a bad block, and says CrosslinkNotReady only means certificate pointers cannot be validated in some way, but it does not tie either point to the refused connections.
options: Port 12301 is a UDP socket, so a TCP 'connection refused' says nothing about the servers, which were still up.
The refusals did matter, but they showed the node was on a side chain, because peers drop nodes whose blocks they cannot link.
The refusals came from the CrosslinkNotReady errors, which mean the node's own BFT certificates were invalid, so peers rejected it.
questions.prompt: In #68 alphiz22 took four BFT peers refusing connections on port 12301 as confirmation that finality was stalled network-wide. What was the answer in #69?

questions.explanation: In #57 samhsmith said that a node with no miner address should mine to its own seed-derived wallet and that the early chain's mining went into the faucet wallet; #60 accepts that the outputs 'aren't mine at all'. The dates cut the other way: #60 says almost all were before June 17, and he only started on June 19. #55 concerned secret.seed files, not these outputs.
options: zk_nd3r's check of the public snapshot, which showed the outputs had arrived through a restored cache rather than from mining.
Shielded Labs confirming that nodes without a miner_address are meant to share one faucet address that nobody controls.
His own check of the dates, which showed the outputs all began after he started mining on June 19.
samhsmith's explanation that tmRB9... is the faucet wallet Shielded Labs' own early nodes mined into, not his node's wallet.
questions.prompt: What changed philthefirst's view of the roughly 43,000 incoming outputs he found on tmRB9... (#60)?

questions.explanation: #62 reports that the transactions could be located but not decrypted with either UFVK, that they do not appear to contain staking actions, that the block hashes do not match its chain and that the mining address is the faucet's. alphiz22 had posted both keys on June 17 (#48), so lateness is not the reason, and #62 says Zingo was still being asked, while confirming staking since block 131,000 for Round 2.
options: The viewing keys arrived after the June 17 deadline, and the screenshots supplied lacked the transaction IDs and block heights that had been requested.
The scan covered only the desktop key, because the mobile key was never submitted and no split of transactions between the wallets was supplied.
Neither submitted key could decrypt the cited Orchard actions, which showed no on-chain staking, and the block hashes and mining address did not match.
The Zingo team had confirmed that the app version used could not produce valid staking transactions, so no earlier staking could count.
questions.prompt: In #62 Shielded Labs explained why it could not verify alphiz22's Round 1 mining and staking. What evidence did it give?

questions.explanation: #104 grants that pauses can be expected and rests the case on duration and documentation, adding that if the duration is expected 'that is useful confirmation as well'; #105 adds the drop in BFT peers. Sl145 explicitly says in #102 that this looks like a network stall rather than a local wallet or mining issue, and never calls the design broken.
options: Any finality pause is a protocol failure, so Shielded Labs should hold the Round 2 payouts until the BFT layer has been properly rewritten and retested.
Because the retargeted bond could not appear in the active roster, the stall proves that Crosslink's delegation design is fundamentally broken.
The stall was caused by a misconfigured local wallet, so restarting mining would have cleared it and the report is mainly a warning to other participants.
Pauses can be expected, but this one lasted hours with PoW advancing about 558 blocks and BFT peers falling from 25-26 to 1, so it is worth recording for developers.
questions.prompt: strahncryptography said finality pauses are common and expected, so questioned whether Sl145's report warranted a post (#103). Which is the strongest argument Sl145 actually made for reporting it (#104, #105)?

questions.explanation: #76 says that from its reading the cited line has no first().expect(), allows that another lib.rs may be meant, and asks for logs and stack traces; it also says the pattern will be marked for replacement. The roster point belongs to #75's own description of the lower-severity findings, #76 stresses safety against adversarial input is necessary for production, and the ZingoDelegator question concerned Round 1 rewards, not crashes.
options: tenderlink already verifies votes against the roster, so a remote peer cannot get a proposal with an empty header list as far as the finality path.
The linked commit has no first().expect() at line 1033 of lib.rs, where the report places the panic, so the diagnosis is uncertain until logs and stack traces are shown.
Prototype code never needs to handle adversarial inputs, so a panic on malformed proposals is not a bug worth tracking at this stage.
alphiz22's node ran an unsupported ZingoDelegator build, so its crashes cannot have come from anything in the finality code.
questions.prompt: alphiz22's security report (#75) said an empty BFT header list panics the finality path and matches the crashes on their node. Which is the strongest case actually made in #76 for caution about that diagnosis?

questions.explanation: #74 begins by saying it is 'not so much' that an incentivized testnet surfaces behaviors a standard one cannot; the main benefit is many more engaged testers. The second option is what ZKZeek restates in #77 while saying 'Agreed'. The third echoes #1's note about matching rewards to the Crosslink design to evaluate incentives, which is a different point from #74's answer.
options: It attracts a much larger group of users who run nodes, report bugs, build tools and share feedback, rewarded for the time and effort they spend.
It surfaces finality behaviors and edge cases that a standard testnet cannot reproduce, because only paid participants generate real load.
It lets Shielded Labs measure whether participants prefer the 40% miner, 40% staker and 20% Dev Fund split over other reward structures.
questions.prompt: ZKZeek asked what an incentivized testnet surfaces that a standard testnet has not (#73). How did Shielded Labs describe its main benefit in #74?
